newsitem.title: USA: Chubb to sell life insurance unit to Jefferson-Pilot.
newsitem.headline: Chubb to sell life insurance unit to Jefferson-Pilot.

text.p: Chubb Corp. said Monday it will sell its Chubb Life Insurance Co. of America to Jefferson-Pilot Corp. for $875 million in cash.

Chubb also is expected to sell its real estate business soon, for an additional $400 million, analysts said. The company said it was making "excellent progress in exploring the options," but provided no details.
The sale of the life insurance unit is part of a stock buyback plan that will allow Chubb to improve profits and launch overseas acquisitions.

For Jefferson-Pilot, based in Greensboro, N.C., the acquisition is a step in its plan to grow faster than its competitors and become one of the largest providers in each of its target product and geographic markets.
The combined companies will have more than 25,000 sales representatives, almost 2 million customers, and more than $160 billion of life insurance in force.

"With the purchase of Chubb Life, our combined companies will rank in the top 15 of life insurance companies nationwide based on total life premium income," said Jefferson-Pilot Chief Executive David Stonecipher.
"Annual life sales will be approximately $200 million, ranking us in the top 10 life insurance companies in the United States for life sales."

Jefferson-Pilot is one of the nation's largest shareholder-owned life insurance companies. Its Jefferson-Pilot Communications Co. owns and operates three network affiliated television stations, 17 radio stations and a sports production company.
In a separate statement, Chubb said the Warren, N.J.-based company intends to use a substantial portion of the proceeds of the sale to buy back its own stock. It gave no details.

Chubb Chairman Dean O'Hare said the management of Chubb Life has "done a terrific job turning the company around in the last two years." But the trend of consolidation in life insurance has created an industry in which scale is increasingly important, he added.
The 115-year-old Chubb had been in the life business since the mid-1950s. Analysts said real estate and life were traditional under-performers for the company.
Peter Wade, vice president at Lehman Brothers, said Chubb's management has been criticised for its inability to maximize the value of the franchise.
Chubb management now realises "they can also boost the value of the company by buying back stock or disposing of under-performing operations," Wade said.
Analysts said Chubb's life unit was a quality operation but one that was too small to post a satisfactory growth rate.

"Basically it was too small to be overall significant to Chubb itself, and it wasn't large enough to have the economies of scale," said Bob Branche, managing partner of Branche Research Group in Philadelphia. "It fits better into a larger life company like Jefferson-Pilot."

Analysts said Chubb was likely to pour more resources into growing its speciality commercial lines -- including directors and officers' insurance, financial institutions insurance and executive protection -- in western Europe and other overseas markets.
Chubb spokeswoman Gail Devlin said the company was "making excellent progress in exploring the options" of its real estate business, but she gave no further details.

The New York Times reported Monday that Chubb was in final negotiations to sell 80 percent of of its real estate business, Bellemead Development Corp., to either Dallas' Patriot American Hospitality Inc. and Boston's Beacon Properties Corp., for about $1 billion, including debt.
The report said it was uncertain which company will win the deal for Chubb's real estate unit.
Chubb's stock rose 87.5 cents to $58.875, while Jefferson-Pilot climbed $1.875 to $59.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
